title.en: Watching the hands of a clock open

text.en:
At 3 o'clock the clock hands make a crisp square corner, at 1 o'clock a narrow wedge, and at 6 o'clock a flat line.
"Every turn makes a different kind of angle!" said Kabir.

An angle measures the amount of turn between two rays meeting at a vertex, measured in degrees (°).
A full turn is 360°, a half-turn straight angle is 180°, and a quarter-turn corner is a right angle of exactly 90°.
An angle less than 90° (between 0° and 90°) is acute. An angle larger than 90° and smaller than 180° is obtuse. A turn larger than 180° up to 360° is a reflex angle.
Whenever two rays meet at a corner point called a vertex, the turn between them forms an angle measured in degrees.

board.text: Angle = turn at a vertex (in degrees °)

text.en: Fold a sheet of paper in half, then in half again neatly—the square corner you create is a Right Angle, always 90 degrees!
Look for 90° right angles everywhere: book corners, classroom windows, and clock hands at 3 o'clock or 9 o'clock.

board.text: Clock at 3:00 makes a 90° right angle

text.en: Now open scissors just slightly—less than a square corner! Any angle greater than 0° and less than 90° is an Acute Angle.
Think of a sharp slice of pizza or clock hands at 1 o'clock or 2 o'clock—nice and narrow, so acute!
Open a notebook wider than an L-corner without flattening it completely—between 90° and 180° is an Obtuse Angle.
Check 4 o'clock or 5 o'clock on a watch face: the hands stretch wider than a right angle, making an obtuse angle.
Open completely into a straight ruler edge at 6 o'clock: two quarter-turns make a Straight Angle of exactly 180°.
And if a hinge bends backward past 180° (between 180° and 360°), that big outside turn is a Reflex Angle; a full circle is 360°.
So compare every angle quickly against a 90° paper corner and a 180° straight edge—acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex!

why.en: 42° is smaller than 90°, so 42° is an acute angle.
90° is an exact quarter-turn square corner, so 90° is a right angle.
135° lies between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse; 180° forms a flat line, so it is a straight angle.

prompt.en: A classmate measures 95° and calls it an acute angle because 95 is close to 90. Why are they mistaken?

requiredIdeas.en: Acute angles must be strictly smaller than 90°.
95° is larger than 90° and less than 180°, so it is already obtuse.
